power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Heterogeneity in infectious disease spread reshapes the risk and severity of outbreaks.
This heterogeneity can arise from intrinsic individuallevel differences in susceptibility, contact patterns, and infectious durations.

Heterogeneity can also emerge from disease dynamics in a canonically homogeneous population, due to the fact that individuals randomly become infected at different times, recover after different intervals, and have access to different numbers of susceptible individuals.
Here, we explore the mechanisms generating emergent heterogeneity by analyzing secondary case distributions within the SIR model.
We show numerically and prove analytically that the variation in secondary cases, calculated over the course of the epidemic, does not change with R0.
This is in contrast to the increasing variation in secondary cases in the linearized SIR model, often used to study heterogeneity at the beginning of an outbreak.
When we consider "forward cohorts" of individuals infected at the same time, between-cohort variation increases as R0 increases, while within-cohort variation decreases.
We show that these effects balance exactly, leading to the invariance of the variation in secondary cases with respect to R0.

These results demonstrate the importance of considering emergent, as well as intrinsic, variation between individuals and of considering heterogeneity of transmission spread over the whole epidemic cycle, including substantive dynamical effects that appear even in the initial outbreak phase.

Real outbreaks have significant heterogeneity in the number of secondary cases -including superspreading, marked by a small fraction of individuals causing a disproportionately large fraction of realized transmission [12, 19].
text.formatted: Real outbreaks have significant heterogeneity in the number of secondary cases -including superspreading, marked by a small fraction of individuals causing a disproportionately large fraction of realized transmission <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19]</ref>.

text.text: Superspreading can help explain why epidemics take off in some situations and not in others, despite apparently similar contexts [4, 11].
text.formatted: Superspreading can help explain why epidemics take off in some situations and not in others, despite apparently similar contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11]</ref>.

text.text: Leveraging knowledge of superspreading can make control efforts more effective [5, 14, 18], especially at the beginning of outbreaks [6].
text.formatted: Leveraging knowledge of superspreading can make control efforts more effective <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18]</ref>, especially at the beginning of outbreaks <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Correspondingly, theoretical treatment of superspreading has emphasized individual-level transmission patterns while assuming a fully susceptible population [9, 12].
text.formatted: Correspondingly, theoretical treatment of superspreading has emphasized individual-level transmission patterns while assuming a fully susceptible population <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref>.

text.text: Models of superspreading often focus on linking observed secondary case counts to a continuous random variable, the individual reproductive number, via a Poisson sampling process.
Canonically, the individual reproductive number is modeled as a gamma distribution, giving rise to negative binomial secondary case distributions [12].
text.formatted: Canonically, the individual reproductive number is modeled as a gamma distribution, giving rise to negative binomial secondary case distributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: In this way, variation arising from the stochastic transmission process is conceptually separated from intrinsic heterogeneity in expected infectiousness that may emerge from potential differences in biology or behaviors between individuals [1, 3, 7].
text.formatted: In this way, variation arising from the stochastic transmission process is conceptually separated from intrinsic heterogeneity in expected infectiousness that may emerge from potential differences in biology or behaviors between individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: Conventional models accounting for heterogeneity typically assume a constant pool of susceptible individuals, implicitly or explicitly focusing on the very beginning of an outbreak.
Over longer timescales, susceptible depletion and replenishment drive population-scale disease dynamics.

Changes in the size of the susceptible population change the proportion of contacts that lead to successful disease transmission and drive differences in expected cases between different cohorts of infectors.

Many deterministic epidemiological models also include explicit heterogeneity, for example by adding compartments for different demographic or geographic groups [17], which can have different average rates of mixing, transmission, or recovery.
text.formatted: Many deterministic epidemiological models also include explicit heterogeneity, for example by adding compartments for different demographic or geographic groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>, which can have different average rates of mixing, transmission, or recovery.

text.text: When implemented in terms of individual events, the inclusion of explicit heterogeneity reproduces superspreading in linear compartmental models [13].
text.formatted: When implemented in terms of individual events, the inclusion of explicit heterogeneity reproduces superspreading in linear compartmental models <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Despite shared theory motivating models that highlight individual-level transmission, and those that emphasize populationlevel transmission dynamics, a gap persists in how each model framework treats individual-level transmission heterogeneity.
The canonical SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Removed) model uses ordinary differential equations (ODEs) to describe disease dynamics.
The SIR model assumes constant, uniform infectivity and recovery times across all individuals during the infectious stage [8, 10].
text.formatted: The SIR model assumes constant, uniform infectivity and recovery times across all individuals during the infectious stage <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10]</ref>.

text.text: Although it appears homogeneous, even the canonical SIR model has two sources of emergent heterogeneity.
First, the changing effective reproductive number arising from susceptible dynamics drives variation between fractions of the population infected at different times.

Second, the exponentially distributed recovery times assumed implicity by the ODE framework drive variation in the number of infections attributable to fractions of the population infected at a given time.
In other words, the deterministic SIR model implies the presence of variation in the expected number of secondary cases.
Here we delineate sources of individual variation in transmission inscribed in simple dynamical models.

We trace how these sources compose into observed or observable heterogeneity in different settings, for example contrasting how heterogeneity emerges in dynamical models versus linearized, or branching-process models.

We begin by revisiting early findings that emergent heterogeneity can drive variation in the secondary case distribution, and discuss how individuallevel heterogeneity has a stronger effect when the basic reproductive number R 0 is smaller.
We then show, first via simulations and then analytically, that emergent heterogeneity in secondary cases is not affected by R 0 across a full SIR outbreak.
Throughout, we highlight the understudied, but critically important, role of disease dynamics per se in generating individual-level heterogeneity.

We aim to spur the development of theory and methods that better integrate heterogeneity and dynamics, ultimately facilitating feedback between data on incidence and individual-level transmission chains, and mechanistic model specification, identification, validation, and intervention design.
The early outbreak phase of an epidemic is modeled using a linearized SIR model, which assumes that the pool of susceptible individuals does not change appreciably.
Early dynamics can thus be characterized by a transmission rate and an infectious period.
Demographic stochasticity generates heterogeneity in this model despite the lack of explicit accounting of individual-level variation in transmission rates and infectious periods.

Since recovery is Markovian, the model implicitly assumes an exponentially distributed infectious period, resulting in an exponentially distributed expected infectiousness (or individual reproductive number) with mean µ = R 0 and generalized dispersion κ = 1.
The resulting distribution of secondary cases is geometric and has a mean equal to R 0 (see Box 1).
text.formatted: The resulting distribution of secondary cases is geometric and has a mean equal to R 0 (see <ref type="bibr">Box 1)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the expected and realized secondary-case distributions are characterized by R 0 (Figure 1a).
text.formatted: Thus, the expected and realized secondary-case distributions are characterized by R 0 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: During the early stages of an outbreak, realized secondary-cases counts are typically modeled using a negative-binomial distribution, with mean µ and shape, or "dispersion," parameter k.
This distribution corresponds mechanistically to a gamma-distributed "expected number of (secondary) cases", with the same mean and shape parameters.

The "realized number of (secondary) cases" is then given by the convolution of this expected number with a Poisson distribution (reflecting necessary, individual-level stochasticity arising from a Poisson contact process) [12].
text.formatted: The "realized number of (secondary) cases" is then given by the convolution of this expected number with a Poisson distribution (reflecting necessary, individual-level stochasticity arising from a Poisson contact process) <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: This is illustrated in Figure 1 for the case where differences in infectiousness arise from random recovery times under simple SIR assumptions, and is thus exponentially distributed.
text.formatted: This is illustrated in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> for the case where differences in infectiousness arise from random recovery times under simple SIR assumptions, and is thus exponentially distributed.

text.text: Expected infectiousness scales exactly with R 0 , so that the smooth curves in Figure 1b, are all the same, but the relative variance in realized cases increases when R 0 is small, because the proportional amount of randomness added by the Poisson step is larger.
text.formatted: Expected infectiousness scales exactly with R 0 , so that the smooth curves in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>, are all the same, but the relative variance in realized cases increases when R 0 is small, because the proportional amount of randomness added by the Poisson step is larger.

text.text: We note a couple of points.
First, the squared coefficient of variation (SCV) of the underlying Gamma distribution is κ = 1/k, so its variance is σ 2  act = κµ 2 .
The resulting variance in secondary-case counts is σ2 = κµ 2 +µ, with the last term arising from the Poisson step of the negative-binomial construction.
In the case of Figure 1, exponentially distributed infectiousness (corresponding to a geometric distribution of secondary cases), κ = k = 1.
text.formatted: In the case of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>, exponentially distributed infectiousness (corresponding to a geometric distribution of secondary cases), κ = k = 1.

text.text: Second, the relationship between σ 2 act and σ 2 holds regardless of the form of the expected infectiousness distribution, due to the Law of Total Variation [16].
text.formatted: Second, the relationship between σ 2 act and σ 2 holds regardless of the form of the expected infectiousness distribution, due to the Law of Total Variation <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: We therefore suggest κ as a generalized dispersion parameter.
This has the advantages of (a) less dependence on a specific assumption about distribution (and parameterization), and (b), the intuitive idea that variation increases when "dispersion" increases.

The heterogeneity in the secondary case distribution means that a large fraction of the initial secondary cases are generated by only a few infectors, even when starting from the canonical homogeneous assumption.

The proportion of expected cases caused by the individuals who remain infectious the longest is the same for any value of R 0 , but the proportion or realized cases caused by the most effective infectors is larger for smaller values of R 0 , since the relative importance of the Poisson infection process increases (Figure 1b).
text.formatted: The proportion of expected cases caused by the individuals who remain infectious the longest is the same for any value of R 0 , but the proportion or realized cases caused by the most effective infectors is larger for smaller values of R 0 , since the relative importance of the Poisson infection process increases (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: As R 0 becomes smaller, an increasing fraction of infected individuals generate no secondary infections, so the individuals who do transmit make up a smaller fraction of all infectors, such that realized heterogeneity is expected to increase as R 0 decreases.
Next we consider the impact of the depletion of the susceptible population during outbreaks on secondary case distributions.
We simulated stochastic SIR epidemics with different R 0 values in a population of 10 4 individuals.
For each infected individual, we recorded the number of secondary cases they generated during the outbreak.
Figure 2 shows realized distributions of secondary cases caused by individual infectors over the entire outbreaks.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> shows realized distributions of secondary cases caused by individual infectors over the entire outbreaks.

text.text: Unlike in the linearized scenario shown in Figure 1, where the susceptible pool remains fully populated, the secondary case distributions, computed across the entire outbreak, appear indistinguishable across a broad range of the key parameter R 0 (compare panel (a) of Figure 1 with the entire set of panels in Figure 2).

text.text: Two key features of the secondary case distributions across an entire outbreak are salient.
First, the mean of the secondary case distribution is approximately 1, as expected.
Since we are considering a single outbreak seeded by a single initial case, the number of infectors must almost equal the number of infectees.
Second, the variance of the realized secondary case distribution is approximately 2, corresponding to a variance of 1 in the expected case distribution, independent of R 0 .
This result is unexpected.
In the absence of susceptible depletion, heterogeneity in expected secondary cases is constant across values of R 0 (Figure 1b).
text.formatted: In the absence of susceptible depletion, heterogeneity in expected secondary cases is constant across values of R 0 (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: During the full epidemic, we expect large-R 0 simulations to cause large dynamical changes, leading to larger variation in expected (and thus realized) secondary cases.
At first glance, it is not clear what could balance the dynamical variation in susceptibles for different values of R 0 to leave the variance constant.

To understand why the heterogeneity in secondary cases over the course of the epidemic is independent of R 0 , we divide the population into "forward cohorts" of individuals infected at the same time, and use variance partitioning to split the heterogeneity into two components: a within-cohort component and a between-cohort component.

Individuals within the same forward cohort have access to the same susceptible pool initially but have differences in their secondary case counts as a result of their exponentially distributed infectious periods.
Individuals in different forward cohorts also differ in the starting size of the susceptible pools that they have access to.

Quantifying heterogeneity in secondary-case distributions helps explain how epidemics unfold and how they can be contained.

Although there have been efforts to quantify individual-level heterogeneity in contact rates [19] and to parameterize biologically realistic secondary case distributions, abstracted from the mechanism [12], these efforts have been largely separate from the construction and evaluation of the compartmental models that enable epidemic forecasting and intervention design (but see [13]).

text.text: Here, we expand the bridge between individual-and population perspectives of heterogeneity by studying epidemiologically-relevant cohorts of infectors that become infectious at the same time.

We first showed how demographic stochasticity and a Poisson contact process result in heterogeneity in secondary cases, even in the linearized SIR model with its canonical assumption of homogeneity between individuals, and lack of susceptible depletion.
Next, we showed how heterogeneity emerges in the SIR model of disease dynamics.

Depletion of susceptibles over the course of an epidemic leads to differences in realized secondary cases between early and late infectors, despite sharing identical underlying infectiousness distributions.
We then found, via simulations, and proved a surprising result -that the total variance in secondary cases over an epidemic is constant across all values of R 0 .

This invariance is unexpected: in the linearized model, relative variance within cohorts is the same across values of R 0 , so we expected the larger betweencohort differences when R 0 is large to drive larger total variance in that case.
Instead, we found the susceptible depletion also drives a corresponding decrease in within-cohort variance.
Our cohort-level analyses reveal the importance of susceptible depletion, even in early stages of the epidemic.
We find that even very early cohorts of infectors have mean secondary case counts much below the theoretical R 0 (Figure 4b).

text.text: This discrepancy becomes larger as R 0 increases.
In practice, this means that mean secondary case counts systematically underestimate R 0 , especially when it is appreciably greater than 1 [15].

text.text: We also showed that the dispersion parameter κ can unify estimates of heterogeneity, without reliance on a particular distributional assumption, across individual-based and compartmental models, particularly beyond the initial outbreak phase, facilitating comparisons with data measured at the individual level.
The independence of the variance in secondary cases hinges on the SIR model structure.
It requires that the infectious period be exponentially distributed.
Further, it requires a well-mixed population.
However, our results with the SIR model provide a baseline for comparing heterogeneity in secondary cases across different compartmental models.

More broadly, by making the implicit explicit, the framework developed here provides a pathway to estimate and incorporate sources of emergent heterogeneity that arise from the dynamics of disease spread, and eventually to combine them with intrinsic individual-level heterogeneity.
We simulated an individual-based SIR model for a population of N individuals.
Each individual was assigned a numerical index and an infectious duration, drawn from an exponential distribution with rate γ.
Next, we built a matrix containing all possible pairs of individuals, and generated a pool of contact events by randomly sampling pairs from this matrix with replacement.
The contact rate for each pair of individuals is β/(N -1), where β is the transmission rate.
The total rate of contact events in the population was obtained by multiplying this rate by the total number of possible pairs, N (N -1)/2, giving βN/2.
The time interval between successive contact events was then drawn from an exponential distribution with a rate βN/2.
Throughout the simulation, we tracked the infection status and number of infections caused by each individual.
We initialized the simulation by assigning a single random individual to be infectious.
We then ran the simulation forward in time, with successive time steps corresponding to successive contact events.
At each time step, we checked the infection statuses of the individuals that came in contact based on when they became infectious and their assigned infectious periods.
If both individuals were susceptible or infectious or recovered/removed, we moved to the next time step.
If one of the individuals was recovered/removed, we moved to the next time step.

However, if one of the individuals was infectious and the other was susceptible, we changed the infection status of the susceptible individual to infectious, noting the time when they became infectious.
We also increased the tally of secondary cases caused by the infectious individual by 1.
Then, we moved to the next time step.
We stopped this process when either no infectious or no susceptible individuals remained.
